 K-pop, K-dramas and kimchi: Inside Judy Joo’s new cookbook
 From "Parasite" to BLACKPINK, the chef brings Korean pop culture-inspired recipes into the kitchen with "Mukja: Let's Eat"
 Judy Joo
 Emli Bendixen
 Words by Daniel Anderson 
 Long before Korean food and culture became a global phenomenon, chef Judy Joo was helping introduce it to Western audiences. A Korean American chef, restaurateur, author and TV personality, Joo built her career across some of the culinary world’s most prestigious kitchens, working with Gordon Ramsay and Heston Blumenthal in London, and Thomas Keller in California. In 2011, she became the first woman to earn the title of Iron Chef UK. 
 For years, Joo has championed Korean food and culture through restaurants, cookbooks and television, finding ways to make the cuisine approachable, while remaining rooted in its traditions. Now, with South Korean culture enjoying unprecedented mainstream attention, she’s taking that mission into a decidedly modern direction with Mukja: Let’s Eat , her latest cookbook that explores Korean food through the pop culture that has helped propel it around the world. 
 Inspired by K-dramas including Extraordinary Attorney Woo and When Life Gives You Tangerines , as well as global K-pop stars such as BLACKPINK and BTS , Mukja: Let’s Eat brings together recipes and the South Korean stories, moments and cultural touchstones behind them. It’s a natural evolution for Joo, connecting the food she has spent decades championing with the dramas and music that have introduced a new generation to South Korea. 
 Joo spoke with JoySauce ahead of the cookbook’s Tuesday release about the inspirations behind the book, her favorite K-dramas, and what this project means to her as a longtime champion of Korean culture.  
 This interview has been edited for clarity and length. 
 View this post on Instagram A post shared by Judy Joo (@judyjoochef) 
 Daniel Anderson: What was the timeline and development process for this cookbook? 
 Judy Joo: About two years in total. It takes about a year just to get the pitch ready, shop it to different publishers, and handle the legal logistics. Once you sign with a publisher, it takes roughly another year to a year and a half to test, edit, print, and publish the book. 
 DA: The book includes references to very recent K-dramas and pop culture phenomena. How did you manage to keep the content so current? 
 JJ: We tried to keep it as current as possible! We managed to include references to K-Pop: Demon Hunters and When Life Gives You Tangerines . Even down to the statistics included throughout the pages, we were constantly revising text right up until deadlines to ensure everything felt fresh and relevant. 
 DA: What was your relationship with K-pop and K-dramas growing up, and how has that evolved over time? 
 JJ: Because I'm a bit older, my early memories of K-pop were groups like Seo Taiji and Boys, Solid, and later Big Bang. Back then, K-pop wasn't in mainstream Western media at all; it was just what we listened to when going clubbing in Korea. 
 As for K-dramas, my mom was always watching them on rented VHS tapes. I really started getting into them myself after college when digital streaming platforms like Viki and DramaFever made international content accessible around 2010. Over time, as Korean media went mainstream globally, I became completely hooked on all the different genres—from classic revenge thrillers like Oldboy to rom-coms and K-horror series like Kingdom . 
 DA: How did you select the recipes and choose which pop culture elements to pair with them? 
 JJ: Some connections were very direct and obvious—like Parasite’s jjapaguri, Squid Game , Crash Landing on You (fried chicken), or Extraordinary Attorney Woo (gimbap). In K-pop, BTS has " Butter ," BLACKPINK has " Ice Cream ," and Jay Park has the " McNasty Burger ." 
 For other recipes, food might play a subtler role in a scene—like the characters hiding out and sharing a simple bowl of gukbap (soup and rice) in Kingdom . Beyond direct pop culture references, I also ensured the book included Korea’s "greatest hits"—essential classic dishes like bulgogi—to keep the collection balanced. 
 DA: How did you approach testing and updating the recipes for this project? 
 JJ: I worked with a culinary producer and recipe tester, Jessica Do. For adapted ideas—like the sweet potato pizza inspired by Hotel Del Luna —we wanted to ensure accessibility for home cooks. We actually bought six popular brands of frozen pizza and tested different sweet potato toppings on them to streamline the recipe. For standard traditional dishes, we focused on refining flavors or adding modern twists, like incorporating specific mushrooms or aromatics to elevate classic profiles. 
 DA: Why did you choose illustrations instead of a traditional photo-only layout? 
 JJ: We wanted the cookbook to feel like a personal scrapbook. It’s a hybrid lifestyle book and cookbook, so we leaned into that nostalgic scrapbook aesthetic. We collaborated with an illustrator based in San Francisco, Asia Kang, to combine photography with vibrant illustrations. She illustrated directly from photos of the finished dishes we sent her to ensure every garnish and detail matched perfectly. The result makes elements pop off the page. 
 DA: You’ve been a long-time advocate for Korean cuisine. How does it feel to see the massive global surge in appreciation for Korean food and culture today? 
 JJ: Growing up, I was sometimes embarrassed by my school lunchbox because I just wanted to fit in with standard American food. Now, I serve Korean food at major venues like Madison Square Garden and Citi Field. Seeing Korean culture celebrated on such a global scale is deeply meaningful. 
 View this post on Instagram A post shared by Asia Kang (@asiakang) 
 DA: What K-pop artists are currently on your personal playlist? 
 JJ: I still love classic old-school acts like Big Bang, but I listen to a lot of current music too—ENHYPEN (their track " Drunk-Dazed " is mentioned in the book), BLACKPINK, Jay Park, and NCT (like " Make A Wish " and " Cherry Bomb "). 
 DA: Which K-dramas or Korean films stand out as your personal all-time favorites? 
 JJ: Oldboy is an absolute masterpiece in cinema history, and The Glory is fantastic for drama. I also love Extraordinary Attorney Woo —Park Eun-bin’s acting range is incredible. Others I’ve really enjoyed include Vincenzo and the comedy film Extreme Job . 
 Published on November 10, 2026 
 Words by Daniel Anderson 
 Daniel Anderson is a disabled Chinese American adoptee based in Seattle. His freelance writing specialties include K-pop, entertainment, and food. He believes that any restaurant can be a buffet, and the key to success is to take a nap each day. Follow his adventures on Instagram @ danzstan .
